meta.blurb: The metal thing in the pit on Horsell Common is too hot to touch, and then its top begins to turn. Within days, Martian machines taller than houses are burning Surrey. One ordinary writer must survive.
meta.bible: Narrator: a writer who lives in Woking, an ordinary man, thoughtful and honest, never named. Wife: the narrator's wife, whom he sends to Leatherhead. Ogilvy: an astronomer at Ottershaw who first sees the Martians. Henderson: a London journalist at the first pit. Stent: the Astronomer Royal. Martians: creatures from Mars, large heads, huge dark eyes, tentacles, a V-shaped mouth, clever and cold. Mars: the red planet, older than Earth and dying. Cylinders: the ten metal capsules that fall from Mars. Heat-Ray: the invisible beam that burns whatever it touches. Tripods: the three-legged fighting machines, taller than houses. Black Smoke: a poison cloud that the Martians fire in shells. Red Weed: the strange red plant that spreads from the pits. Horsell Common: the sandy common near Woking where the first cylinder lands. Woking: the narrator's town in Surrey. Surrey: the county south of London. Chobham: a village near Woking. Weybridge: a town on the River Thames. Shepperton: a town on the Thames. Thames: the river. Leatherhead: where the narrator's wife stays. Sheen: where the narrator hides in a ruined house. Putney Hill: where the narrator meets the Artilleryman. Primrose Hill: where the narrator finds the last Martians. London: the great city. Curate: a weak, frightened clergyman who hides with the narrator. Artilleryman: a soldier with big dreams of living underground. Brother: the narrator's brother, a medical student in London. Mrs Elphinstone: a lady whom the brother helps. Miss Elphinstone: her young sister-in-law. Thunder Child: a brave ironclad ship of the Royal Navy. Ulla: the Martians' cry. Bacteria: the tiny germs that kill the Martians. Voice and tone: calm, serious and vivid, told after the event by one who survived; the horror is real but never gory; the end brings quiet relief and thoughtfulness. Added in the full-length book: Ottershaw: the village where Ogilvy has his observatory. Winchester: the town over which the green shooting star is seen. Maybury: the part of Woking where the narrator lives, with Maybury Hill behind it. Spotted Dog: the inn whose landlord lends the narrator a horse and dog-cart. Edgware: the north London road where the brother meets the ladies. Chelmsford: the Essex town where they buy food. Regent's Park: the London park beside Primrose Hill. St Paul's: the great domed cathedral that the narrator sees over London in the morning light.

beats.scene: A quiet English garden at night with the red planet shining above

beats.scene: A dry red desert world under a small, pale and distant sun

beats.scene: The narrator walks home across the heath as the sun rises over pines

beats.summary: A train goes by, full of calm passengers who know nothing about the common.

beats.scene: A policeman under a street lamp looks at a man's burned coat
beats.summary: A policeman looks at his burned coat and tells him to go home and rest.

beats.scene: A man opens a garden gate; the lit windows of a house glow ahead
beats.summary: At last, he reaches his own gate and sees the lit windows of his house.

beats.summary: His wife runs out to meet him, frightened by his torn and dirty clothes.

beats.summary: They sit down to a late supper, but he cannot eat, and they speak in whispers.

beats.summary: At dawn, soldiers arrive on the common and form a wide ring around the pit.

beats.summary: The narrator warns an officer about the Heat-Ray, but the officer only smiles politely.

beats.scene: Neighbours chat over garden fences with newspapers in their hands
beats.summary: Woking goes on with its day, and people are more curious than afraid.

beats.scene: Men in a garden laugh and point toward the distant common
beats.summary: Everyone says that a few shells will soon finish the slow, weak creatures.

beats.scene: A man at a window watches green lights flicker above a dark common
beats.summary: The hammering goes on, and the narrator becomes sure that the Martians are building something.

beats.summary: The narrator tells his wife to go to her relatives in Leatherhead.

beats.summary: He borrows a horse and a dog-cart from the landlord of the Spotted Dog.

beats.scene: A cart on a twilit road; a woman looks back at a red glow

beats.summary: A flash shows a huge shape on three legs, far taller than any house.

beats.summary: The machine strides over the pine trees like a man through grass.

beats.summary: When he wakes, the mare is dead and the machine has gone.

beats.summary: From his study window, he sees a pillar of smoke rising from Maybury.

beats.summary: A wounded artilleryman crawls into the garden, black with smoke.

beats.scene: A soldier eats bread at a kitchen table while a man pours water
beats.summary: The narrator gives him water and bread, and he tells how his comrades were killed.

beats.summary: Another machine comes down the road toward the house, and the two men run out the back.

beats.summary: At a crossroads, the artilleryman goes to find his battery, and the narrator goes on alone.

beats.summary: A Martian machine wades into the Thames, with water up to its knees.

beats.summary: The fallen machine cries out and beats the water, but it cannot rise.

beats.scene: A man crawls onto a reedy bank while a town burns behind
beats.summary: He crawls out onto the far bank, and the little town burns behind him.

beats.scene: A scalded man walks along a riverbank past broken boats and burned houses
beats.summary: Weak and scalded, the narrator walks along the bank past wreckage and burned houses.

beats.scene: An empty village street, with open doors and small garden fires
beats.summary: The village of Shepperton is empty, with open doors and small fires burning.

beats.scene: A thin pale man in black sits crying by the roadside
beats.summary: He meets a curate, a thin, pale man who sits by the road asking what it all means.

beats.scene: A thin man in black waves his arms at a red evening sky
beats.summary: The curate says the end of the world has come, but the narrator says it is a war.

beats.scene: Two men walk along a river road, one weeping and one grim
beats.summary: The narrator is tired of his weeping, but he cannot leave him, so they go on together.

beats.scene: Two men eat bread and cold meat at a table in a deserted house
beats.summary: In an empty house, they find bread, meat and wine, and they eat in the half dark.

beats.scene: Two men at a window look at a distant machine against a red sky
beats.summary: Through the window, they see a Martian machine far away, and they sit very still.

beats.scene: A man sits awake at night thinking about a wife far away
beats.summary: The narrator thinks of his wife, but the Martians hold the road, so he must go around.

beats.scene: Two figures creep along a dark lane and hide in a ditch
beats.summary: At night, they leave the house, hear a far cry, ulla, and hide in a ditch.

beats.scene: Dawn light on an empty road, two tired men walking on
beats.summary: At dawn, they walk on, and the curate's weeping makes the narrator think of leaving him.

beats.summary: In London, the narrator's brother, a medical student, reads about the creatures on the common.

beats.scene: A thin, dirty man sits in the shade of a tree on a hill
beats.summary: On Putney Hill, he finds a man sitting under a tree, and it is the artilleryman.

beats.scene: A soldier speaks bitterly, his hands moving in the air
beats.summary: The artilleryman says mankind is beaten and the Martians will keep the survivors in cages.

beats.scene: A man points at a drain opening beneath a city street
beats.summary: He says the only safe place is under the ground, in the drains and tunnels of London.

beats.scene: A man draws an underground city with lamps and books in the dust
beats.summary: The artilleryman dreams of a hidden city below the earth, and of taking the world back.

beats.scene: A shallow hole in the ground and a pack of cards on the grass
beats.summary: The narrator sees that the artilleryman is only a dreamer, and he says goodbye.

beats.scene: A lone man walks down a wide silent London street between shuttered shops
beats.summary: The narrator walks into London and finds the streets empty and the shops shut.

beats.scene: Black dust lies on empty pavements and a door swings in the wind
beats.summary: A thin black dust lies over the streets, and nothing moves in the city.

beats.scene: A man stops in an empty street and turns his head to listen
beats.summary: Far ahead, he hears a long, sad cry: ulla, ulla, ulla.

beats.scene: A man stands among tall houses listening to a sound that has no source
beats.summary: The cry rises and falls and seems to come from the whole dead city.

beats.scene: A man sits alone on a doorstep, thinking of home
beats.summary: He sits down and thinks of his wife, and the loneliness is worse than fear.

beats.scene: A man stands up from a doorstep, brushing dust from his coat
beats.summary: He decides that he would rather meet the Martians than live alone and afraid.

beats.scene: A man walks down a street with his empty hands held out
beats.summary: He walks on with open hands, and the cry grows louder and more broken.

beats.scene: A giant black machine towers over the trees of a green park
beats.summary: At the edge of Regent's Park, he sees a giant Martian machine that does not move.

beats.scene: Dark birds circle a silent machine and settle on its hood
beats.summary: He waits behind a wall, and a flock of birds settles on the still machine.

beats.scene: A man in sunlight looks up at the hood of a motionless machine
beats.summary: He creeps closer and finds the Martian inside the machine dead.

beats.scene: A great pit on a grassy hill with still dark shapes at the bottom
beats.summary: On Primrose Hill, he finds a huge pit with more dead Martians in it.

beats.scene: Tall machines stand motionless across a vast city under a clear sky
beats.summary: From the hill, he sees the great machines standing motionless across London.

beats.scene: Dogs and dark birds gather on the grass beside a silent machine
beats.summary: Dogs and birds have come to feed on the dead, and the narrator turns away.

beats.scene: A soldier's rifle and a broken gun lie in a trampled field
beats.summary: He remembers how nothing could stop the invaders, and wonders why they have died.

beats.scene: The dome of a great cathedral rises above a city in morning light
beats.summary: In the morning light, the dome of St Paul's rises clear above a city free of smoke.

beats.scene: Scientists study a glass slide beside a microscope in a bright room
beats.summary: Scientists explain that the Martians were killed by the smallest living things on Earth.

beats.scene: A long line of people through history, then a single great black machine
beats.summary: Mankind has long learned to live among germs, but the Martians had no defence.

beats.scene: A red field of weed turning grey and brown on a hillside
beats.summary: The red weed from Mars also withers, and the English fields turn green again.

beats.scene: A man sits weeping on a grassy hill as a city wakes below
beats.summary: The narrator weeps with relief, and the city slowly begins to wake.

beats.scene: A woman brings tea to a man asleep in a clean bed
beats.summary: A kind family finds him ragged and takes him into their home.

beats.scene: A family at a table with newspapers and tea, a man reading aloud
beats.summary: At the family's table, he hears that the Martians have died all over the world.

beats.scene: A crowded railway platform with a steam train and smiling people
beats.summary: Trains run again, and the telegraph carries the good news around the world.

beats.scene: A man on a train looks out at fields turning green again
beats.summary: The narrator takes a train toward Woking, and he fears what he will find.

beats.scene: An open front door, a silent hall and a desk with a page
beats.summary: He returns to his house in Woking and finds it silent and empty.

beats.scene: A man at a desk turns at the sound of a voice behind him
beats.summary: He hears a step and a voice, and he turns around, afraid to hope.

beats.scene: A man and woman hold each other in a doorway
beats.summary: His wife is alive, and the couple are reunited and deeply thankful.

beats.scene: A Martian machine in a great hall, with scientists looking up at it
beats.summary: The Martian machines are put on show, and scientists study them.

beats.scene: A boy looks at a globe and a night sky full of stars
beats.summary: People learn that Earth is small, and he wonders if men will reach Mars.

beats.scene: Neighbours help each other carry boxes along a quiet town street
beats.summary: People grow more careful and kind, but the narrator still dreams of the black machines.

beats.scene: A man and his wife in a garden at sunset, a lit window behind
beats.summary: He looks at the sun and the ordinary world with new eyes and is grateful.

A1A2: Long ago, people on Earth were calm, but minds on Mars were watching them.
Mars was older than Earth, and it was getting cold and dry.
The Martians looked at Earth, which was warm, green and full of water.
Ogilvy was an astronomer, and he worked at night at Ottershaw.
Ogilvy let the narrator look at Mars through the big telescope.
One night, Ogilvy saw a bright flash of gas jump from Mars.
The newspapers printed a few lines, but most people did not care.
The flashes came again every night, ten nights in all.
Ogilvy said it was very unlikely that men lived on Mars.
The narrator went home to Woking, and life stayed calm and ordinary.
A bright green star crossed the night sky, and many people saw it.
The narrator watched the green light fall behind the dark pine trees.
At first light, Ogilvy walked across the common to look for it.
He found a wide, deep hole in the sand, with broken trees around it.
In the hole lay a huge metal tube, and it was too hot to touch.
Henderson came, then the narrator, and they stood beside Ogilvy at the edge.
Ogilvy saw that the end of the tube looked like a lid.
Then they heard a soft scraping sound coming from inside the hot metal.
Ogilvy and Henderson ran to Woking to send telegrams to London.
The narrator walked home for breakfast, thinking hard about the strange thing.
News of the pit ran through Woking, and many people hurried there.
Workmen dug around the tube, and it was bigger than they thought.
Boys threw stones at it, and the crowd acted as if it were a holiday.
Stent, a famous scientist, came to look at the tube with Ogilvy.
Some people said it came from Mars, but many people only laughed.
That night, a few men sat by the pit with their lanterns.
On the second day, more people came, and the common looked like a village fair.
At sunset, the narrator went back, and hundreds of people stood around the pit.
The scraping grew louder, and the whole crowd leaned closer to the pit.
The people at the back pushed, and Stent begged them to stand back.
The end of the tube began to turn slowly, with a loud scraping sound.
A man cried that someone was inside, but the heat drove people back.
At last, the lid fell off and hit the sand with a crash.
In the dark hole, two shining discs, like eyes, looked at the crowd.
A grey arm, thin like a snake, rose out of the dark.
A big grey creature rose up, with huge dark eyes and a strange mouth.
It was heavy and weak, so it slipped and fell back inside.
The crowd screamed and ran, and the narrator ran too until he fell.
The narrator hid behind a bush, afraid, but he could not stop looking.
Three brave men stayed, and they tied a white cloth to a stick.
The small group walked down toward the pit, holding the white flag high.
A little green light shone, and green smoke rose from the pit.
Something like a mirror rose from the pit, and it shone brightly.
A beam of fire swept over the sand, and the brave men burned.
Trees, bushes and the white flag all burst into flames.
The beam swept across the road, and people ran and screamed.
The narrator lay flat on the ground, and the fire passed over him.
He jumped up and ran, with burning trees falling around him.
He rolled into a deep ditch, and the fire did not reach him.
He lay there shaking, and he knew the Martians were clever and cruel.
When the fire died down, he climbed out and walked toward home.
At the edge of town, people asked him what all the noise was.
He told them about the creatures, but they thought he was mad.
A train went by, full of calm people who knew nothing.
A policeman looked at his burned coat and told him to go home.
At last, he reached his gate and saw the lights of home.
His wife ran to him, afraid of his torn and dirty clothes.
He told her everything and said the Martians were weak on Earth.
They sat down to a late supper, but he could not eat.
From the window, they saw a red glow, and heard hammering far away.
At dawn, soldiers came and made a ring around the common.
They set guards around the pit, and nobody could go near.
The narrator warned an officer about the Heat-Ray, but the officer only smiled.
Neighbours talked over their fences, and Woking went on with its day.
Everyone said a few big guns would soon finish the weak creatures.
But the sounds from the pit went on, and the narrator grew afraid.
The narrator told his wife to go to her relatives in Leatherhead.
His wife did not want to go, but she packed a small bag.
He borrowed a horse and a cart from the landlord of the Spotted Dog.
They drove away along the road, as the light began to fade.
They drove toward Leatherhead, and his wife looked back at the red glow.
At Leatherhead, her relatives welcomed her, and the quiet street seemed safe.
The narrator kissed his wife at the gate and promised to send word.
He fed the mare, and he saw dark clouds growing in the sky.
On the way back, the storm broke, with loud thunder and heavy rain.
The mare was afraid of every flash, and the road became a river.
A flash showed a huge shape on three legs, taller than any house.
It walked over the pine trees like a man walking through grass.
The mare ran wild, the cart turned over, and the narrator fell.
When he woke, the mare was dead, and the machine was gone.
He got up and limped home through the storm and broken trees.
In a flash, he saw more machines walking across the fields toward the river.
He hid under a hedge, and he heard a strange cry, ulla, ulla.
He saw that it was a machine, with a hood on top.
At dawn, the storm ended, and the narrator reached his home.
The house was empty and silent, and a clock ticked in the hall.
From his window, he saw the valley, and smoke rising from Maybury.
A soldier, black with smoke, crawled into the garden, and he was hurt.
The narrator gave him water, and he told how the soldiers had died.
They saw another machine coming, so they ran out the back door.
At a crossroads, the soldier went to find his guns, and they parted.
At Weybridge, the road was full of people with carts and bundles.
Soldiers put big guns beside the river, hoping to stop the Martians.
A Martian machine walked into the river, with water up to its knees.
A gun fired, and the machine fell into the river with a big splash.
The fallen machine cried out, but it could not stand up again.
More machines came and turned their fire on the soldiers and the water.
The Heat-Ray swept the river, and the water boiled into hot steam.
The narrator jumped into the river and swam under the hot steam.
He crawled onto the bank, and the burning town was behind him.
He walked along the bank, past burned houses and broken boats.
The village was empty, with open doors and small fires burning.
He met a curate, a thin man who sat by the road crying.
The curate said the end of the world had come.
The narrator was tired of his crying, but they walked on together.
In an empty house, they found bread and meat, and they ate.
From the window, they saw a machine far away and stayed still.
The narrator wanted to find his wife, but the road was blocked.
At night, they heard a far cry, ulla, and hid in a ditch.
At dawn, they walked on, and the curate still cried and prayed.
In London, the narrator's brother read about the strange creatures in the paper.
He thought the story was silly, and the papers made too much of it.
The streets were calm, church bells rang, and nobody seemed worried.
In the evening, a boy shouted that the Martians were destroying whole towns.
People crowded outside newspaper offices to read the news, and fear began.
Wild stories spread about poison smoke and walking machines near London.
The brother counted his money and packed a small bag.
The railway stations were full, and the trains could not carry everyone.
A long line of people was leaving the city on foot.
The brother joined the crowd and walked north, out of London.
On the road north, rich and poor walked together, running from the same fear.
Carts broke down and bags fell, but nobody stopped to help.
At Edgware, he saw bad men attacking a small carriage with two ladies.
The brother ran forward, fought the men, and drove them away.
The ladies were Mrs Elphinstone and Miss Elphinstone, and they thanked him with tears.
They asked him to drive, and he took the reins.
They drove through the night with thousands of other frightened people.
They rested beside the road, and the brother kept watch.
In Chelmsford, bread was very costly, but the brother bought some.
They heard that ships were leaving the coast, so they hurried east.
At the coast, he saw the sea full of ships and small boats.
A huge crowd was trying to leave, but the boats were few.
The brother gave a man all his gold to row them out.
The little boat took them to a big steamer full of people.
On deck, hundreds of people sat among their bags, waiting to leave.
At last, the steamer sailed, and England became a thin line behind.
Out at sea, three huge Martian machines walked toward the ships.
A big black ship, the Thunder Child, rushed at the Martians.
Her guns knocked one machine down, but the Heat-Ray set her on fire.
The other ships escaped, while the brave ship burned behind them.
They followed the river to Sheen, where the fields were quiet and empty.
They found a house with a garden, and they went inside to rest.
At night, a green light shone in the sky above the house.
A green star fell down from the sky with a great noise.
It hit the garden, and the house broke and fell on them.
The narrator woke in the dark, covered with dust and badly hurt.
They crawled into a small room, the only part still standing.
Through a hole in the wall, the narrator saw a huge pit.
In the pit, the Martians were making new machines out of bright metal.
He saw that they used the fresh blood of living animals as food.
They hid in the dark for many days with little food.
The narrator counted the days by the grey light on the wall.
He watched the Martians through the crack, and learned how they worked.
One day, a finished machine walked out of the pit and away.
The curate could not stay quiet, and he talked all day long.
They had very little water, and the curate drank too much.
The curate began to shout, and the narrator was afraid the Martians would hear.
A long metal arm came into the room and moved about.
The narrator hid in the dark, and the arm took the curate away.
After fifteen days, all was quiet, and the pit was empty.
He climbed out of the ruined house into the bright morning air.
He found some food in a broken kitchen and ate it slowly.
A strange red plant was growing all over the broken ground.
The red plant grew along the river and over the fields.
He walked toward London, and no birds sang anywhere along the road.
On Putney Hill, he met a thin man sitting under a tree.
It was the artilleryman, and he said that men were beaten.
The artilleryman said that people must now live under the ground.
He dreamed of a safe city under the ground, full of books and lights.
The narrator saw that the man only talked, so he walked away.
He walked into London, and the streets were empty and quiet.
A thin black dust lay on the road and on the roofs.
Then he heard a long, sad cry: ulla, ulla, ulla.
The cry went up and down, and it came from far away.
He was tired and alone, and he wanted to see another face.
He decided that it was better to meet the Martians than wait alone.
He walked on with his hands open, and the cry grew louder.
At last, he saw a huge Martian machine standing still in the park.
The machine did not move, and now the strange cry had stopped.
Inside the machine, the Martian was dead, and the narrator laughed.
He climbed Primrose Hill and found a pit with dead Martians.
All over London, the great machines stood still and silent.
Birds and dogs came to feed on the dead Martians.
No army had stopped them, so the narrator wondered why they died.
In the morning light, he saw the dome of St Paul's.
Later, he learned that tiny germs had killed the Martians.
The Martians had no way to fight the germs of Earth.
Soon the red plant began to die and turn grey.
The narrator wept with joy, and the city slowly woke up.
A kind family found him and gave him food and a bed.
The family told him that the Martians had died everywhere.
Soon the trains ran again, and people came back to London.
The narrator took a train to Woking and walked to his house.
The house was silent, and his desk was just as he left it.
Then he heard a voice, and he turned around quickly.
His wife was alive, and they held each other and cried.
The Martian machines were put on show, and scientists studied them.
People learned that Earth was small and that life could come from space.
People were kinder now, but the narrator still dreamed of black machines.
He looked at the sun and was thankful for every ordinary evening.
B1B2: In the last years of the nineteenth century, people believed that nothing could disturb the peace of their small world. Yet across space, minds far older and colder than ours were studying the Earth and making their plans.
Mars is a much older world than ours, and it has been cooling for a very long time. Its people can see that their planet is slowly dying, and the sight fills them with fear.
The Martians look across space at the warm, green Earth, which is so much richer than their own dry world. Slowly and with great patience, they begin to plan how to take it.

Ogilvy is a well-known astronomer who lives and works at Ottershaw, a few miles from the narrator's town. On clear nights, his observatory stands open to the stars, and the narrator often visits him there.
One night, Ogilvy lets the narrator look through the telescope at the planet Mars. It is a tiny, round, orange disc, and it seems very still and very far away.
Soon afterward, Ogilvy sees a jet of glowing gas burst out from the edge of the planet. He sends telegrams to other astronomers, and they hurry to their own telescopes to look.
The newspapers print a few short lines about the flash on Mars, and then they forget it. Most people, busy with their own lives, never read the notice at all.
The flashes come again the next night, and the next, ten nights in all. Ogilvy believes that some mighty explosion is throwing the gas up from the planet, but he cannot be sure.
As they talk in the dark, the narrator asks whether living creatures might have made the lights. Ogilvy laughs kindly and says that the chances of men on Mars are about a million to one against.
The narrator returns to his house in Woking and goes back to his work and his quiet evenings. Nobody in the town suspects that anything has changed, and the flashes are soon forgotten.
Late one night, a bright green shooting star crosses the sky over Winchester and Surrey. Many people see it, and most of them think it is only a meteor falling to the ground.
From his study window, the narrator sees the green light drop behind the dark pine trees. He thinks it is an ordinary meteor, and soon he puts out his lamp and goes to bed.
Ogilvy, who has seen the star fall, is sure that it landed somewhere close by. At the first grey light of morning, he walks out alone across Horsell Common.
On the sandy common, he finds a wide pit that has been torn into the ground. The sand is thrown up in great heaps, and the nearby fir trees are broken and burned.
At the bottom of the pit lies a huge cylinder, dark and scaly, half buried in the sand. It is far too hot to touch, and the air above it shakes with heat.
Henderson, a journalist from London who lives nearby, soon joins him, and the narrator arrives a little later. The three men stand together at the edge of the pit, speaking in low voices.
Ogilvy notices that the end of the cylinder looks like a lid, with a rim running all the way around it. He realises that it cannot be a rock from space, because somebody has made it.
While they stare, a faint sound of scraping comes from inside the hot metal. The three men look at one another, and nobody wants to say what he is thinking.
Ogilvy decides that the news is too important to keep, and he hurries off to Woking with Henderson. There, they send telegrams to the great London newspapers and to the astronomers.
The narrator walks home across the common as the sun rises over the pines. At breakfast, he tells his wife about the strange thing in the pit, but he does not yet understand what it means.
News of the strange pit runs through Woking, and by the afternoon crowds are hurrying across the common. Shopkeepers close early, and families bring their children to see the sight.
Workmen arrive with spades and begin to dig around the cylinder to free it. As the sand falls away, they see that it is much bigger than anyone had imagined.
Boys throw stones at the cylinder to see whether anything will happen, and the crowd laughs. People treat it like a holiday show, and nobody seems to be afraid.
Stent, the Astronomer Royal, arrives to examine the cylinder together with Ogilvy and Henderson. They walk around the pit again and again, whispering and making notes.
Ogilvy tells the others that the cylinder may have come from Mars, and he reminds them of the flashes. Most of the crowd laughs at him, and a few shake their heads sadly.
Night comes, but a few men stay beside the pit with lanterns to watch the silent metal. Nothing happens, and by midnight even the most curious go home to bed.
On the second afternoon, the crowd is larger than ever, and the common looks like a village fair. Carts, bicycles and children fill the road, and the heat makes everyone thirsty.
As the sun sinks, the narrator goes back to the common for one last look. Hundreds of people are standing around the pit, and there is a strange hush over the heath.
Then the scraping begins again, louder than before, and the whole crowd leans closer to listen. The narrator feels a cold shiver, although the evening is still warm.
The people at the back push forward to see, and the ones at the front are almost forced into the pit. Stent and Ogilvy beg everybody to stand back, and slowly the people give them room.
In the last red light of the sun, the end of the cylinder begins to turn slowly. A harsh, rasping sound comes from it, as if a giant screw is being undone from the inside.
A man in the crowd cries out that there must be somebody inside who needs help. Brave people move forward to open the cylinder, but the heat of the metal drives them back.
At last, the lid drops from the cylinder and rolls down into the sand with a ringing crash. A black hole opens in the end of the metal, and a deep silence follows.
In the dark mouth of the cylinder, two shining discs appear, like the eyes of some animal. The narrator, who is standing near the front, cannot look away from them.
A thin grey arm, like a snake, rises out of the darkness and feels the air. A second one follows it, and the narrator's blood turns cold.
Then the creature itself rises into the light, grey and shining, and as big as a bear. It has huge dark eyes and a wet, V-shaped mouth without any chin, and it breathes in heavy gasps.
The creature is clumsy and heavy under the pull of the Earth, which is stronger than that of Mars. It struggles to the edge of the cylinder, slips, and falls back with a wet groan.
The crowd screams and runs, pushing and falling over one another in the half dark. The narrator is carried along with them until he trips over a root and falls.
He crawls behind a bush and lies there, shaking, with his face turned toward the pit. He is terribly afraid, but he is also too curious to look away.
A few brave men have stayed near the edge, and Stent, Ogilvy and Henderson are among them. They tie a white cloth to a stick, because they hope to speak with the creatures in peace.
Under the last light of the sky, the little party walks slowly down toward the pit. Stent and Ogilvy walk in front, and Henderson holds the white flag high above his head.
A faint green light flickers in the mouth of the pit, and a puff of green smoke rises silently into the air. The narrator, watching from behind his bush, feels a sudden fear for the men.
Then a shining shape like a round mirror rises slowly above the edge of the pit. A strange, dazzling light begins to tremble in it, and it grows brighter every moment.
A beam of heat, which nobody can see, sweeps across the sand toward the men. In an instant they are wrapped in flames, and they fall without a cry.
Everything the beam touches bursts into fire, from the bushes and the heather to the pine trees along the road. The whole common seems to leap into flame, and the night turns as bright as day.
The beam swings across the road, and the roof of a house breaks into flames. People run screaming in all directions, and some of them are caught by the light as they run.
The narrator throws himself flat on the ground, and the Heat-Ray passes just above his head. He feels a wave of heat on his back, and the smell of burning is everywhere.
As soon as the beam turns away, he jumps to his feet and runs as fast as he can. Burning branches fall around him, and sparks fly into the sky like angry insects.
He rolls down into a deep ditch, where the wind of the fire cannot reach him. He lies at the bottom, gasping for breath and covered from head to foot in sand.
As he lies in the ditch, the narrator understands what he has seen. The Martians are clever, they have no mercy, and a flag of peace means nothing to them.
When the fire begins to die down, the narrator climbs out of the ditch and staggers toward home. His coat is scorched, his hands are bleeding, and he walks like a man in a dream.
At the edge of Woking, a few people stand at their garden gates, asking each other what the noise was. They have heard shouting from the common, but they have seen nothing.
The narrator tells them about the creatures and the Heat-Ray, and he warns them to leave. They stare at his black face and decide, politely, that he must be mad.
A train goes by on the line beyond the road, with its windows full of light. The passengers are reading their papers and talking quietly, and not one of them knows what has happened.
A policeman looks at the narrator's burned coat and his wild eyes. He listens for a moment, shakes his head, and advises him to go home and rest.
At last, the narrator reaches his own gate on the hill and sees the lamplit windows of his house. They look so warm and so ordinary that he nearly weeps.
His wife runs out to meet him, white with fear, and she holds him as if he might disappear. She has heard strange rumours in the town, and she has been watching the road for an hour.
Sitting at the table, he tells her everything, and he adds that the Martians may be weak on Earth. Their bodies are made for a lighter world, and he hopes they will never climb out of the pit.
A late supper is set on the table, but the narrator cannot eat more than a few mouthfuls. They talk in low voices about the creatures, and his wife tries hard to be brave.
Later, at the window, they see a red glow low over the dark common. From very far away comes a faint sound of hammering, which goes on and on.
At dawn, soldiers arrive on the common with horses and rifles, and they form a wide ring around the pit. The people of Woking, who have never seen so many soldiers, come out to stare at them.
Officers set guards around the ring, and nobody is allowed to go near the pit any more. Behind the guards, soldiers are digging trenches where they can hide with their guns.
The narrator speaks to an officer and warns him about the Heat-Ray and the white flag. The officer thanks him politely, but it is clear that he thinks the story is a little exaggerated.
In the town, newspapers print only a few lines, and neighbours chat over their garden fences. Life in Woking goes on almost as usual, and people are more curious than afraid.
Everyone says that the soldiers will soon deal with the creatures, which look weak and slow. A few well-aimed shells, they say, will finish the whole business before the end of the week.
But the narrator can hear the hammering from the pit, and at night he sees strange lights above it. He becomes certain that the Martians are building something, and he cannot sleep.
At last, the narrator decides that his wife must go away from Woking for a few days. He tells her to go to her relatives in Leatherhead, which is a safe distance from the common.
His wife does not want to leave him, and they argue gently for an hour. In the end, she agrees, and she begins to pack a small bag with a sad face.

The narrator walks to the Spotted Dog to ask the landlord for a horse and a dog-cart. The landlord is reluctant, because horses are scarce, but the narrator pays well and promises to bring the cart back that night.
The cart rolls away from the house with the narrator's wife sitting beside him and her bag at her feet. The light is fading, the road is empty, and for a long time nobody speaks.

They drive on toward Leatherhead through the warm dusk, and the narrator's wife looks back at the red glow over the common. Neither of them speaks, because both of them are thinking about the same thing.
At Leatherhead, her relatives are surprised to see them so late, but they welcome her warmly. The street is quiet, the lamps are lit, and everything there seems calm and safe.
The narrator kisses his wife at the gate and promises to send word as soon as the soldiers have finished. She holds on to his hand a moment longer than usual, and then she lets go.

He gives the mare some water and a short rest, and he notices dark clouds piling up in the sky. He decides to drive back that night, because he has promised to return the cart and he wants to be at home.
On the road back, the storm breaks, with loud thunder and flashes of blue-white light. The rain comes down so hard that the narrator can hardly see the road in front of him.
The mare is frightened of every flash, and she pulls at the reins while the road turns into a river. The narrator speaks to her gently and holds on, because he does not want to be thrown.
Then a long flash lights up the hill, and he sees a huge shape standing on three legs. It is taller than the houses, and it is walking across the countryside as if the ground were nothing.

The machine strides over the young pine trees like a man walking through grass, and the trees break under its metal feet. The narrator cannot breathe, and for a moment he forgets that he is holding the reins.
The mare bolts in terror, and the cart goes racing down the road until it hits a ditch and turns over. The narrator is thrown out, and he lies on the wet ground, stunned and bruised.
