They seemed to look at him, and through him, and into the world beyond.

A thin grey arm, glistening and supple like a snake, rose out of the darkness and swayed in the air, as if feeling for the shape of a strange world. A second arm followed the first, and then a third, and the narrator felt his blood turn cold in his veins. Somebody behind him began to whimper in a thin, high voice, and no one in all that crowd told him to stop.

Then the creature itself rose into the light, grey and shining and about as large as a bear, with its skin wet like leather in the rain. It had huge dark eyes, a lipless mouth shaped like a V that dripped with moisture, and no chin at all, and it breathed in heavy, labouring gasps. The sight was so strange and so ugly that the narrator's mind refused it for a moment.

The creature was clumsy and heavy under the pull of the Earth, which is much stronger than the pull of Mars, and every movement seemed to cost it a painful effort. It struggled to the edge of the cylinder, slipped on the smooth metal, and fell back out of sight with a wet, groaning cry. For a long moment, nobody on the common moved or spoke, and the only sound was the faint hiss of the cooling metal.

Then the crowd broke, and people screamed and ran in every direction, pushing and falling over one another in the half dark, as hats and bicycles and picnic baskets were flung aside. The narrator was carried along in the rush until his foot caught in a root and he went sprawling on his face. When he rose, he found himself alone on the cold sand, with his heart thumping and the shouts already fading in the dusk.

He crawled behind a thick bush of gorse and lay there, shaking all over, with his face turned back toward the pit and its dark edge. He was more afraid than he had ever been in his life, but he was also too curious, and too stunned, to look away. Someone had to see what happened next, and it seemed that he was the one.

A few brave men had not run away but stayed near the edge of the pit, and Stent, Ogilvy and Henderson were among them. They tied a white handkerchief to the end of a stick, for they hoped that the creatures were reasonable beings who might be spoken to in peace. They thought, as most people would have thought, that anything so clever must also be kind.

Under the last gleam of the sky, the little party moved slowly down the slope toward the pit, with Stent and Ogilvy a few steps in front. Henderson held the white flag high above his head, so that no one could mistake it, even in that fading light. From behind his bush, the narrator watched them go and felt his heart go with them.

A faint green glow flickered in the mouth of the pit, and a puff of green smoke rose silently into the still air, drifting up toward the first stars. The three men stopped for a moment, uncertain, and then walked on again, still holding out their flag. The narrator, who was watching, felt a sudden terror for them that he could not explain.

Then a shining shape, like a round mirror of polished metal, rose slowly above the edge of the pit and turned a little, as if it were looking for something. A strange light began to tremble in its surface, and it grew brighter and brighter, until it hurt the eyes. The narrator could not guess what it was, but every instinct told him that it was a danger.

A beam of heat, which no one could see, swept across the sand toward the little group of men, and in an instant they were wrapped in flame. They fell without even a cry, and where they had stood there was only a patch of smoking ground. The white flag was gone, and with it went every hope of a peaceful meeting between the two worlds.

Everything the beam touched burst into fire, from the dry heather and the tall bushes to the pine trees along the road and the fences beside it. The whole common seemed to leap into flame at once, and the night turned as bright as noon. The narrator saw it all in a single dreadful moment, and he never forgot the sight.

The beam swung slowly across the road, and the roof of a house broke into flames, as if a giant had touched it with a torch. People ran screaming in all directions, and some of them were caught by the light as they ran, and fell. It was not a battle at all, because only one side had a weapon, and that side was not on the Earth.

The narrator threw himself flat on the ground, pressing his face into the sand, and he felt the Heat-Ray pass over his head like the breath of an enormous furnace. The smell of burning was everywhere, and the heather around him began to smoke and crackle. He lay there for a moment without the strength to move, certain that the next sweep of the beam would be his last.

As soon as the beam had turned away, he jumped to his feet and ran, with no thought in his head except to put distance between himself and that dreadful pit. Burning branches fell around him, sparks flew up into the sky like angry insects, and the heat scorched his back. He ran like a hunted animal, blind and gasping, and he did not look behind him.

He tumbled down the side of a deep ditch, where the wind of the fire could not reach him, and lay at the bottom, gasping for breath and covered from head to foot with sand. Above him, the sky glowed red, and the burning heath roared like the sea in a storm. He pressed himself against the earth and prayed that no one would find him.

As he lay in the ditch, the narrator understood at last what he had seen: the creatures from Mars were clever, they were armed with a terrible weapon, and they had no mercy at all. A flag of peace meant nothing to them, because they did not look upon men as equals, but as creatures that stood in their way. He shook all over, and for a long time he could not think of anything else.

When the fire at last began to die down, the narrator crawled out of the ditch and stumbled toward home along the road, bruised, blackened and shaking in every limb. His coat was scorched, his hands were bleeding, and he walked like a man in a dream, hardly knowing where his feet were taking him. Behind him, the red glow of the burning common seemed to follow him all the way along the dark road.

At the edge of Woking, a few people stood at their garden gates, asking each other what all the noise had been about. They had heard the shouting from the common and the far-off crackle of the flames, but they had seen nothing with their own eyes. To them, it was still only an uproar, as strange and as harmless as a fair.

The narrator told them, as clearly as he could, about the creatures and the Heat-Ray, and he warned them to leave their houses while there was time. They stared at his blackened face and his wild eyes, and then, with great politeness, they decided that the poor man had gone out of his mind. One of them even offered him a chair and a glass of water, as one might to a child who had woken from a bad dream.

A train went rattling by on the line beyond the road, with its windows full of yellow light and its carriages full of people who were reading their newspapers and talking quietly. Not one of those passengers knew what had happened on the common, and the narrator watched them go with a strange, sick envy. For them, it was still an ordinary evening in the ordinary world, and the narrator felt that he no longer belonged to it.

A policeman, standing at a corner under a lamp, looked at the narrator's burned coat and bleeding hands, and he listened to the first few words of the story with a patient face. Then he shook his head and advised the narrator, kindly but firmly, to go straight home and lie down. It was exactly what the narrator longed to do, and yet he had never been less able to rest.

At last, the narrator reached his own gate on the hill and saw the lamplit windows of his house shining through the trees. They looked so warm and so ordinary, so completely unaware of what lay behind him, that for a moment he could hardly bear to look at them. He pushed open the gate with a trembling hand, and he went up the path.

His wife ran out to meet him, white with fear, and she held him as though he might disappear into the night if she let him go. She had heard strange rumours in the town from the neighbours, and she had been watching the road for the better part of an hour. When she saw his torn and dirty clothes, she did not ask a single question.

Sitting at the table, he told her everything, from the first scraping to the last flash of the Heat-Ray, and he added that the Martians might be weak on Earth. Their bodies, he explained, were made for a lighter world, and the pull of our planet must feel to them like a crushing weight. He hoped, with all his heart, that they would never be able to climb out of the pit.

A late supper was set on the table, but the narrator could not eat more than a few mouthfuls, and his wife, too, only pushed the food around her plate. They talked in low voices about the creatures, the flag and the three men, and she tried hard to be brave for his sake. Outside, the night wind rattled the windows and stirred the trees in the garden, and neither of them felt safe in their own house.

Later, when the house was quiet, they stood together at the window and looked out toward the common, where a red glow lay low against the dark sky. From very far away came a faint sound of hammering, steady and patient, like the noise of a workshop that never sleeps. The narrator did not tell his wife what he thought it meant, although he was almost sure that he knew the answer.

At dawn, soldiers arrived on the common with horses, guns and rifles, and they formed a wide ring around the pit, a good distance from its edge. The people of Woking, who had never seen so many men in uniform, came out of their houses to stare, and some of them waved. For the moment, the whole affair seemed more like a parade than a war.

Officers set guards along the ring and gave orders that nobody was to approach the pit any more, whatever excuse they might have. Behind the line, soldiers were busy digging shallow trenches where they could lie hidden with their guns and wait. It was a sensible plan, but it was made for an enemy of the kind that soldiers already knew.

The narrator found an officer and told him earnestly about the Heat-Ray, the white flag and the three men who had died. The officer thanked him politely and wrote a word or two in his notebook, but it was plain that he thought the tale a little exaggerated. A man who has seen a miracle should not expect to be believed in a hurry.

In the town, the newspapers printed only a few lines, and the neighbours chatted over their garden fences, trading rumours and opinions with the greatest enjoyment. Life in Woking went on almost as usual, for people were more curious than frightened, and the shops stayed open as always. A stranger passing through the town that afternoon would have guessed nothing at all about the thing waiting on the common.

Everyone said that the soldiers would soon deal with the creatures, which were slow, weak and clumsy, and which could not even leave their pit. A few well-aimed shells, they said, would finish the whole business, and the town would sleep in peace before the end of the week. The narrator listened to them with a heavy heart, and he wished with all his strength that he could believe what they said.

But the narrator could hear the hammering from the pit going on without a pause, and at night he saw strange green lights flicker above the sand. He became certain that the Martians were building something, and that they were building it quickly, with the patience of minds that never tire. Sleep would not come to him that night, and he lay awake for hours listening to the faint, steady, patient sound from the dark.

At last, the narrator decided that his wife must go away from Woking for a few days, until the danger was past. He told her to go to her relatives in Leatherhead, which lay a safe distance from the common, where she could wait quietly until he sent word. He told himself that it was only a precaution, and he almost believed it.

His wife did not want to leave him, and for an hour they argued gently, as married people do when each of them is afraid for the other. In the end, she gave way, because she saw that he was in earnest, and she began to pack a small bag with a sad and thoughtful face. It was a quiet and rather sad business, and neither of them had much to say while the clothes were folded into the bag.

The narrator walked to the Spotted Dog and asked the landlord for a horse and a dog-cart, but the landlord was unwilling at first, because horses were scarce that day. The narrator paid him well and promised to bring the cart back that same night, and at last the landlord gave in. It was a small bargain, and it was the beginning of a very long night.

The cart rolled away from the house with the narrator's wife sitting beside him, her bag at her feet and her hands clasped tightly in her lap. The light was fading, the road lay empty before them, and nobody spoke for a long time. Behind them, on the hill, the little house stood quiet, with its windows turning dark.

They drove on toward Leatherhead through the warm dusk, and the narrator's wife looked back over her shoulder, again and again, at the red glow that hung above the common like the reflection of some distant furnace. Neither of them spoke, because both of them were thinking about the same thing, and neither wished to be the first to say it aloud. The horse trotted steadily on, and the hedges went by in the gathering dark.

At Leatherhead, her relatives were astonished to see them arrive so late, but they welcomed the narrator's wife warmly and drew her into the lighted hall. The street was quiet, the lamps were burning, and everything about the place seemed calm, respectable and safe, as if no creature from Mars could ever disturb it. It was hard to believe that such a peaceful town existed in the same world as the burning common.

The narrator kissed his wife at the gate and promised that he would take care of himself and send word as soon as the soldiers had finished their work. She held on to his hand for a moment longer than usual, and then, very slowly, she let go. He climbed back into the cart with a tight feeling in his chest, and he did not look round, for fear that he might change his mind.

He gave the mare some water and a short rest in the stable of the house, and as he did so, he noticed that dark clouds were piling up in the sky, heavy with rain and thunder. He decided to drive back that night, because he had promised to return the cart, and because he could not bear the thought of waiting in a strange house while his own lay in danger. The air was thick and hot, and a few big drops had already begun to fall.

On the road home, the storm broke at last, with a crash of thunder that seemed to split the sky, and flashes of blue-white light that turned the night into noon for one dazzling moment at a time. The rain came down so hard that the narrator could hardly see the road in front of him, and in a few minutes he was soaked to the skin. It was, he thought, the worst weather that he had ever driven through, and it seemed to him that the whole sky was angry.

The mare was frightened of every flash and pulled at the reins with all her strength, while the road turned into a stream of brown water beneath the wheels. The narrator spoke to her softly and held on with both hands, because he did not want to be thrown, and he could feel her whole body shaking. Somewhere ahead of them, in the darkness beyond the hedges, there was a heavy, rhythmic sound that was not thunder at all.

Then a long flash lit up the hill beside the road, and the narrator saw a huge shape standing on three legs against the sky, far taller than any house. It was made of shining metal, and it carried a kind of hood at the top, and it was walking across the countryside as if the ground itself were nothing. He stared at it with his mouth open, and then the whole world went dark again.

The thing strode over the young pine trees as a man strides through tall grass, and the trees snapped and fell beneath its metal feet with a sound like a gunshot. Its long cords hung down in front of it and swung gently as it walked, and each of its steps shook the earth. The narrator could not breathe, and for a moment he forgot that he was holding the reins.

The mare bolted in terror, and the cart went racing down the road in the blinding dark until it struck the edge of a ditch and turned over with a crash. The narrator was thrown clear and lay on the wet ground, stunned, bruised and gasping, with the rain beating on his face. For a time he did not know where he was, or how long he had lain there.

When he came to himself, the rain was still falling, and the mare lay dead beside the broken cart, and the thing on three legs had gone. But the narrator knew very well that it had not gone far, and that the Martians were no longer prisoners in their pit. He sat up in the mud, and he understood that the war had begun.

The narrator struggled to his feet, with his head aching and his clothes streaming, and he limped toward home through the storm, which was beginning to weaken at last. All around him the pine trees were broken and bent, as if a mighty hand had swept through them, and the road was littered with branches. He walked as a man walks who has been beaten, but he walked on.

By the light of the flashes, he saw more of the machines far across the fields, walking in a line toward the river, and each of them moved with the same slow and terrible grace. They were like giants who had woken in the night and set out upon some business of their own, and there was nothing in the whole country that could stop them. The narrator watched them from the dripping hedge with his heart thudding so loudly that he thought it must be heard.

He hid under a hedge and held his breath as one of the machines passed close by, and from somewhere high above him there came a strange, howling cry, which sounded like ulla, ulla, ulla. It rose and fell, mournful and wild, and it was answered from a long way off by another voice just like it. The narrator knew that he would remember that sound for the rest of his life.

Close at hand, he could see that the thing was a machine and nothing more, made of shining metal and walking on three legs, with long cords swinging from its body like the arms of an octopus. At the top there was a hood, with room enough in it for a living creature, and the narrator shuddered when he thought of what might sit inside. It was then that he understood that the Martians had come to ride over the Earth, and not merely to creep upon it.

At dawn the storm ended at last, and the sky above the broken pines turned a grey and gentle colour, as though nothing had happened in the night. The narrator, cold and tired and covered with mud, found his way along the road to his own house on the hill. He had never in all his life been so glad to see a chimney, a gate and a garden wall, and he almost laughed.

The front door stood open, and the house was silent and empty, with the grey light of morning lying across the floors. In the hall a clock was still ticking, and on the table in the dining room the supper dishes stood just as they had been left on the evening before. It felt like a place from a story that someone else had told about a different time.

He climbed the stairs to his study and looked out of the window across the valley toward the common and the town. A great pillar of smoke was rising from Maybury, and the rising sun shone through it with a dull red light, and the whole country seemed to be holding its breath. He stood quite still for a long time, and he did not know what to do.

While he was watching, a soldier crawled through the hedge into the garden below, black with smoke and plainly hurt, and he lay down on the grass like a man who can go no farther. He was an artilleryman, and the narrator, forgetting his own fear, hurried down the stairs to help him. The soldier looked up at him with red and weary eyes, and tried to smile.

The narrator gave the soldier water, bread and a chair in the kitchen, and while the man ate, he began to tell his story in short, broken sentences. His guns had been set on the slope near Maybury, he said, and the Martians had killed his comrades in a single moment, with no warning at all. He alone had escaped, by hiding in a ditch where the fire did not reach him.

While the artilleryman was still speaking, the two men heard a heavy tread outside, and from the window they saw another machine coming down the road toward the house, its hood swinging from side to side. They did not wait to see more, but ran out through the back door, across the garden and into the fields. Behind them, the great shape grew larger and darker with every step that it took, and the ground trembled under their feet.

At a crossroads, the artilleryman said that he must find what was left of his battery and fight again, and nothing the narrator said could change his mind. The two men shook hands there in the grey morning light, as men do who think they may never meet again, and the soldier turned toward the guns. The narrator went on alone toward the river, and the road seemed longer than it had ever been.

Weybridge was full of frightened people, pushing carts and wheelbarrows piled high with chairs, clocks and bundles of clothes, and the road was blocked with horses that had been pulled into the wrong lanes. Some were crying, some were shouting for lost children, and some walked in silence with white, set faces. The whole place looked like an ant's nest that has been kicked by some careless giant, and the noise of it was dreadful.

Soldiers were placing guns on the bank beside the Thames, and they hoped with all their hearts to stop the Martians at the river, which the creatures would have to cross. The narrator stood a little way back and saw that the men were nervous but quite determined, and that their officers spoke in low and careful voices. Nobody there yet knew how little a gun could do against such an enemy.

A tall Martian machine came striding down the course of the river, with the water up to its knees and a trail of white foam behind it, and it stooped now and then as if it were searching for something. Its hood turned slowly from side to side, and the cords dangled from its body and dipped into the stream. The narrator crouched behind a low garden wall with his mouth dry and his hands cold, and he did not dare to move.

A gun fired with a deafening crack, and a shell burst against the hood of the machine, which staggered, spun round and fell sideways into the river with a splash as tall as a house. A great cry went up from the soldiers on the bank, and some of them threw their caps in the air. For a moment, it seemed to the narrator that the whole war had turned, and that men had learned how to kill the giants.

The fallen machine uttered a terrible, howling cry and beat the water with its cords in a blind fury, and waves of mud and steam rolled across the river from the struggle. The creature was hurt and could not rise, but even in its pain the narrator felt a kind of awe at the sheer size of the thing. He thought that no animal on the Earth, however large or however angry, could ever have made such a noise.

For one brief moment, the soldiers cheered, because one of the Martians was down, and a few of them even began to laugh with joy. Then, through the smoke, other machines appeared, three of them side by side, and they turned their beams upon the guns and the soldiers and the river. The cheering stopped as if it had been cut with a knife, and a terrible silence settled over the river bank.

The Heat-Ray swept across the river, and the water began to boil in great rolling clouds of steam that hid the whole scene in a white and roaring mist. Boats burned, the willows crackled, and the air was so hot that the narrator felt his skin tighten and his eyes sting. He did not stop to think, because there was nothing left to do but run.

The narrator threw himself into the river and swam under the steam as best he could, with his head low and his arms working, and he felt the water grow hotter by the second. It was almost too hot to bear, and his hands and his face began to burn, but the boiling mist hid him from the machines. He swam as he had never swum before in all his life, and he did not once lift his head to see what followed.

At last, he crawled out onto the far bank, half dead with pain and fear, and lay among the reeds with his face in the mud, shaking all over. Behind him the Martians were striding away across the river, one after another, and the little town was burning like a torch. For a long time he could not even lift his head to look, and the only sound that he could hear was the roar of the fire.

The narrator, weak and scalded and wrapped in his wet clothes, walked along the river bank among the wreckage of boats and the blackened walls of burned houses, with every step costing him an effort. Now and then he stopped to rest, and each time it became harder to rise and go on. The sun was already hot above him, and the whole valley smelled of smoke and of wet, burned wood.

He came to the village of Shepperton, where there was not a living person to be seen, and the doors of the houses stood wide open on empty rooms. Small fires were burning here and there in the gardens, and the clothes lay on the lines as if the owners had only stepped out for a moment. It was the stillest and saddest place that he had ever seen, and the silence pressed on his ears like a weight.

At the end of the street, he saw a thin, pale man dressed in black, sitting by the roadside and crying like a child, and when he came nearer, he saw that the man was a curate. The curate looked up at him with red and frightened eyes, and he asked, over and over, what all this meant, and why it had been sent to them. The narrator had no answer to give him, and he was not sure that any answer existed.

The curate said that the end of the world had come, and that God had turned his face away from men, and that every sin they had ever committed was now being paid for. The narrator, who had seen too much that night to be patient, answered that this was a war and not a punishment, and that men would have to fight it. The curate stared at him as if he had spoken in a foreign tongue.

The narrator was very tired of the curate's weeping and his endless talk, but he could not bring himself to leave a helpless man alone in such a place. So the two of them walked on together along the road beside the river, the one silent and grim, the other murmuring prayers under his breath. Neither of them knew where they were going, or what they would find when they got there.

In an empty house at the edge of the village, they found bread, cold meat and a bottle of wine, and they ate like hungry children, standing at the table in the half dark. The owners had left in such a hurry that a cup of tea still stood on the table beside the plates. The narrator felt that he was a thief, and yet he was also very grateful.

Through the window of the house, they saw a Martian machine standing far away against the red evening sky, as still and as upright as a lamp-post. They sat down very quietly in the dark, and even the curate, for once, kept his lips closed. It stood there for what seemed like hours, and then slowly it turned and moved away over the fields.

All through that night the narrator thought of his wife, who was safe, he hoped, in her relatives' house in Leatherhead, and who might at that moment be thinking of him. But he had heard from other refugees that the Martians held the road to the south, and he knew that he must go around by the river and London. It was a long way, and every mile of it was full of danger.

In the middle of the night, they left the house and crept along the lane with a bundle of food, keeping close to the hedges. Far away, they heard the howling cry of the Martians, mournful and strange, and they hid in a ditch until the sound had faded. The curate trembled so violently in the dark that the narrator could hear his teeth chattering, and he had to hold his arm to keep him quiet.

At dawn, they were walking again, and the curate was crying and praying once more, in a voice that grew weaker and more broken with every mile. The narrator began to think that he would do better alone, and that the man was a burden he could not afford to carry. And yet, for some reason that he could not explain, he did not leave him.

In London, the narrator's brother, a young student of medicine, sat in his rooms and read the newspaper account of the strange creatures that had come to Horsell Common. The report was short and a little vague, and it seemed to him like some far-fetched story invented to fill a quiet column. He read it twice, and then he turned to the page about the weather.

He put down the paper and smiled, because he could not believe that such a thing could be real, and he thought that the editors were making a great deal out of very little. Like almost everyone in the capital, he had never imagined that the ordinary world might be threatened from outside. His coffee grew cold on the table while he sat and pondered the matter, and then he forgot about it altogether.

The streets of London were calm, the church bells were ringing across the rooftops, and families walked in the sun in their best clothes, as they had always done on a fine day. Nobody in the great city seemed to be worried, or even very curious, about what had happened in a distant county. It was a pleasant day in a world that did not know what was coming.

In the evening, a newsboy ran along the street shouting that the Martians had destroyed whole towns on the Thames, and people hurried from their doors to buy a copy. The brother pushed through the crowd, snatched a paper, and read the black headlines under the gas lamp with a cold feeling in his stomach. For the first time, he felt truly afraid of what the morning might bring.

Crowds gathered outside the newspaper offices to read the latest telegrams as they were pinned to the walls, and they pushed and pressed against one another to see. Each new line told of another village burned, another army lost, and another gun silenced, and the faces of the readers grew whiter and whiter. Even those who had laughed at the news that morning no longer laughed, and some of them began to speak of leaving.

Wild stories began to spread through London, of machines that walked on three legs, of a ray that burned whole streets, and of a poison smoke that killed everyone who breathed it. Nobody knew which of these stories were true, and the fear grew with every hour that passed. By midnight, the city that had been so calm and so sure of itself was whispering and trembling in the dark.

The brother counted his money on the table, packed a small bag with a few clothes and a loaf of bread, and decided that he must leave London while there was still time. He stood for a moment in the doorway, looking back at his books and his narrow bed, and wondered whether he would ever see his rooms again. Then he locked the door behind him with a steady hand, put the key in his pocket, and went down the stairs and out into the street.

At the railway stations, thousands of people pushed and shouted, trying to find a place on any train that would carry them out of the city, and the platforms were choked with trunks, bags and crying children. The trains were full long before everyone had found a seat, and many people were left standing at the barriers, staring at the empty rails. It was the first time that the brother had ever seen what real panic looked like, and he hoped that it would be the last.

A long line of people began to leave the city by every road, some on foot, some on bicycles and some in carts piled with furniture, and the sound of their going was like the murmur of a river. They carried bags, boxes and bundles, and the children walked at their sides and asked in small voices where they were going. Nobody had an answer that was fit to give them, and most of the parents simply said that they would know when they got there.

The brother joined the crowd on the northern road and walked out of London, with his bag over his shoulder and his heart beating hard in his chest. Behind him, the great city waited in the darkness, full of fear, under a sky dim with smoke and the glow of distant fires. He did not look back, because he knew that he could not bear to.

On the road to the north, rich and poor walked side by side, all running from the same fear, and the sound of their feet and wheels rose up like the roar of a distant sea. Carriages, bicycles, carts and wheelbarrows pushed along together in a cloud of choking dust, and the horses were wild with thirst. No one spoke except to complain, to curse, or to ask the way to somewhere safer, and nobody could tell them.

Carts broke down, and bags and boxes fell into the road, but nobody stopped to help, because everybody was thinking only of himself and of the creatures that might be coming up behind. The brother saw a woman sitting alone on a trunk with her hands in her lap, and no one so much as looked at her. It was a new and bitter lesson in how people behave when they are afraid.

At Edgware, the brother saw a small carriage stopped in the road with two ladies sitting in it, and three rough men were pulling at the pony and trying to take it away. The ladies were crying out for help, but the crowd walked by on both sides without looking, like water around a stone. The brother did not stop to think about the danger, because he could not bear to walk past them like all the others.

He ran forward and struck the nearest man hard in the face, and after a short and confused fight, in which he took a cut lip and bruised hands, he drove the three men off. They ran away into the dusty crowd, swearing and holding their heads, and the pony stood trembling in its harness. The brother stood there too, breathing hard, with his lip bleeding, and astonished at what he had done and at how little he had feared.

The ladies, who were Mrs Elphinstone and her young sister-in-law, Miss Elphinstone, thanked him with tears of relief and held out their hands to him. They were alone, they told him, and they did not know where to go or what to do, and no one else in the whole crowd had offered to help them. He answered, as gently as he could, that he was glad to be of use, and that anyone would have done the same.

They begged him to take the reins, because their hands were shaking too much to hold them, and he agreed at once, for he did not like to leave them alone in such a crowd. Together they decided to go to the coast, where they hoped to find a ship that would carry them away from England. The pony, as if it understood, lifted its head and set off along the road.

They drove all through the night with thousands of other frightened people, and the road was a river of dust and noise and tired faces in the light of the lanterns. Now and then a rumour ran along the line that the Martians were close behind, and the whole crowd quickened its pace for a little while. Then, slowly, the fear faded again, and it gave way to a dull weariness that was almost worse, and the road went on.

At last they stopped beside the road to rest, and the two ladies fell asleep in the carriage, their heads against each other, while the brother kept watch with a stick across his knees. All around them he could hear voices murmuring, children crying, and the shuffle of tired feet that never seemed to cease. He sat there until the stars began to fade, and he never once closed his eyes.

In Chelmsford, food was scarce and prices were very high, but the brother bought bread and cheese and a little milk with the ladies' money, and he paid whatever was asked of him. They ate quickly in the carriage, among shouting crowds, and the bread tasted better than any he had ever known. Even in the midst of such a terrible flight, hunger remained hunger, and a simple meal could still seem a kind of happiness.

Presently they heard that ships were taking people away from the coast, and that every steamer that could float was gathering at the mouth of the river, and they hurried east toward the sea with new hope. The ladies held on to each other, and the pony trotted bravely on through the heat of the day. For the first time since they had set out, they thought that they might be saved.

At the coast, the brother beheld a strange and wonderful sight, for the sea was full of ships, steamers and small boats, as far as the eye could see. Smoke rose from their funnels into the sky, and their flags hung limp in the heat, and all of them waited for people to climb on board. It looked like a great fleet that had come to take away a whole nation.

A great crowd stood on the shore, pushing and shouting, and everyone wanted to be on the next boat. There were only a few small boats, and the boatmen asked such prices that only a few people could pay, while the rest stood in the water and looked on in despair. The brother, who had seen many sad things in the last few days, found that he could hardly bear this one.

The brother paid a boatman with almost all the gold that he had, and the man, after counting it twice, agreed to take them out to a steamer lying at anchor in the bay. The two ladies climbed into the boat with the help of the brother's strong arm, and the little craft pushed off from the beach. Behind them, voices called and begged, and the brother did not turn his head.

The small boat moved slowly through the crowded water toward a large steamer, rocking in the wash of other vessels, and the boatman pulled at his oars with a grim face. Many hands reached down to lift them over the side, and before long they had found a place on the crowded deck. The ladies sat down at once, pale and silent, and the brother stood beside them.

On the deck, hundreds of people sat among their bags and bundles, and nobody had room to stretch out a hand. A child cried in a thin voice, an old man prayed aloud, and a woman held a canary in a cage on her lap, and all of them waited for the last passengers to come aboard. It was a floating village of frightened strangers, who had nothing in common except the fear that had driven them from their homes.

At last, the steamer began to move, and the low, flat coast of England slowly sank into the haze behind them, like a country in a dream. The brother stood at the rail, unable to believe that he was leaving his own land, and perhaps for ever. A gull flew over the ship and cried, as if nothing in the world had changed.

Out at sea, three huge Martian machines suddenly appeared, walking through the waves toward the ships with long, slow strides, and they were so tall that the water reached only to their knees. The captain of the steamer shouted an order, and the engines throbbed faster, but a steamer full of passengers could not run away from such giants. Every face on deck turned toward the sea, white with horror, and for a long moment nobody on the crowded steamer spoke or moved.

Then, from behind the steamers, a long, low ironclad called the Thunder Child rushed forward with smoke pouring from her funnels and the white foam standing high at her bows. She went straight toward the enemy at full speed, like a hunting animal that has no thought of being afraid, and the people on the steamers watched her in silence. For a moment, even the Martians seemed to hesitate, as if they could not believe that anything on Earth would dare to face them.

Her guns roared, and one of the great machines fell into the sea in a cloud of steam, but a flash of the Heat-Ray struck the ship and set her on fire from end to end. Burning, she still drove forward, with her flag flying, and her gunners kept firing until the very last moment. It was the bravest thing that the brother had ever seen, and he knew that he would remember it for the rest of his life.

While the Martians were busy with the ship, the steamers slipped away over the water, and the brother watched the brave ironclad vanish in a cloud of smoke and fire. He stood at the rail for a long time, silent, thinking of his brother, and wondering whether any man in England would ever stand on dry land again. Then the ladies called him, and he turned away from the rail, because there was nothing more that any man could do.

The narrator and the curate followed the river toward Sheen, through a countryside so quiet and so empty that it seemed to have been abandoned for centuries. On both sides, the houses stood broken and roofless, and the gardens were trampled into mud by the passage of some enormous weight. The only sound was the slow murmur of the water, which went on flowing as though nothing in the world had changed.

At the edge of the village, they came upon a house standing in a garden that the Martians had somehow overlooked, with its windows unbroken and its doors still shut. The neighbouring cottages lay in ruins, their roofs open to the sky, and the contrast made the survivor feel uneasy rather than glad. Nevertheless, they were weary beyond words, and they went inside to find shelter for the night.

They climbed to a room at the top of the house, and the narrator stood at the window, looking out across the dark and silent land. Far above the rooftops, the sky had begun to glow with a strange green light that grew brighter with every passing minute. He could not tell what it was, but a cold dread settled in his stomach, as it had done on that first night upon the common.

Without any warning, a green star came rushing down out of the sky, and a roar like a great gale filled the night. The earth leapt under their feet, and the windows shattered, and the curate screamed aloud in terror, as the whole house shook like a ship in a storm. The narrator had just time to understand that another cylinder was falling, and that it was falling very near.

The cylinder struck the garden beside the house with a force that tore the building apart, and the walls leaned inward and came down in a roaring cloud of brick and plaster. Beams and tiles rained upon the narrator, and a heavy blow upon his head sent him spinning into blackness. Of what happened next he knew nothing at all, for he lay as still as the dead among the ruins.

When at last he woke, he found himself lying in a stifling darkness, half buried in dust and rubble, with a cut upon his head and an ache in every limb. Close beside him, he could hear the sound of ragged breathing, and he realised with a rush of relief that the curate had also lived. For some time neither of them moved or spoke, as men do who are not yet sure that they belong to the world of the living.

Slowly and painfully, they dragged themselves over the broken floor to a small room at the back of the house, which was the only part of the building that had not fallen. The curate whimpered at every movement, and the narrator, though his own body was sore, kept a firm grip on the man's sleeve lest he wander off in the dark. There they sat down together among the dust and the silence, hardly daring to breathe and listening to the groan of the timbers overhead.

In the wall of the little room, the narrator discovered a long crack where the bricks had parted, and after a moment's hesitation he put his eye to it. Beyond lay an enormous pit, raw and freshly dug, with the grey light of dawn creeping over its edge. At the bottom of it, half buried in the churned earth, lay the dark cylinder that had destroyed his shelter.

Inside the pit, the Martians were hard at work, and the narrator found that, in spite of his horror, he could not take his eyes away from them. With the help of curious jointed engines that moved like living hands, they were putting together tall new machines out of a pale metal that gleamed like silver. It was a scene of tireless, patient, terrible skill, and it told him more clearly than any argument that he was watching an enemy who did not mean to go away.

Then he saw something that he would never be able to forget, for the Martians were feeding, and their food was the fresh blood of living creatures. He drew back from the crack, sick and trembling, and for a long while he lay with his face against the cold bricks. The curate asked him what he had seen, and the narrator, out of mercy and exhaustion, answered only that it was better not to look.

For many days the two men lay hidden in the darkness, with scarcely any food, and the hours crawled by with a slowness that seemed almost deliberate. The narrator kept count of the days by the grey light that came through the crack in the wall, scratching a mark each morning upon the plaster. Time had lost its meaning, and he began to feel that the whole of his former life had happened to another man in another world.

They had only a few crusts of bread and a little water, and hunger soon began to gnaw at them both, making their limbs heavy and their tempers short. The narrator, who was the stronger of the two, rationed what remained with a care that the curate resented bitterly. Each hour seemed longer than the last, and the silence of the ruined house grew thick with unspoken fear.

Whenever he could, the narrator crept to the crack and watched, and little by little he came to understand the habits of the invaders. Their strange engines did the heavy work with an ease that no human labourer could have matched, while the creatures themselves hardly seemed to rest or to sleep. It struck him that they were not cruel in the way that men are cruel, but merely single-minded, as a flood is single-minded.

On the fifth day, a new fighting machine rose above the edge of the pit, tall and gleaming on its three jointed legs, and stood as though testing its strength. Then it strode away across the fields with long, gliding steps, and the ground trembled faintly under the ruined house. The narrator wondered where it was going, and he felt a shiver of dread for the people who lay in its path.

The curate could not be quiet, and from morning until night he muttered and whispered to himself, praying or complaining in a thin, wandering voice. The narrator asked him again and again to stop, but each time the man fell silent for only a few minutes before he began once more. It was like living beside a leaking tap, and it wore on the narrator's nerves until he longed to be alone.

One morning, the narrator discovered that the curate had secretly drunk most of their little water while he slept, and a bitter quarrel broke out between them in the darkness. They argued in furious whispers, for neither dared to raise his voice, and in the end the narrator took charge of what bread was left. From that day, there was no trust between them, and each watched the other with a wary and sullen eye.

Soon the curate began to shout aloud, declaring that the Martians were a punishment sent upon the world for its sins, and that they must all be ready to die. The narrator, with rising alarm, begged him to be silent, for the noise might carry through the hole in the wall to the very creatures from which they were hiding. But the curate seemed no longer to hear him, and he raved on, with his eyes wide and wild in the half light.

Without warning, a long metal arm came sliding through the hole in the wall, and it began to feel its way slowly about the little room. The narrator flung himself back into the darkest corner, where a heap of coal and rubbish lay, and covered his face with his arms. He did not dare to breathe, and in the stillness he could hear the faint and horrible scraping of the metal on the floor.

The arm found the curate, who was still crying out in his madness, and it closed upon him and drew him away through the wall. His voice rose once in a long, thin cry, and then the sound was cut off, and the narrator knew that he would never see the man again. For hours afterward, he lay in the coal and the dark, trembling in every limb, until at last he was sure that the thing had gone.

For two more days he stayed hidden, eating the last of the scraps and listening, and then, on the fifteenth day, the sounds of work stopped altogether. When at last he crept to the crack, he found the great pit quiet, and as far as he could see, the Martians were gone. A stillness that he had almost forgotten lay over the ruined land, and he dared at last to hope.

At last the narrator pushed his way out of the ruins and stood blinking in the bright morning air, after almost two weeks of darkness. The sunshine hurt his eyes so sharply that he could do nothing for some minutes but sit among the bricks with his hands over his face. When he looked up again, the world appeared at once familiar and utterly changed, like a house in which somebody has died.

In the wrecked kitchen of a neighbouring house, he found a loaf of bread and some tins that the owners had left behind, and he ate slowly, fighting the wish to swallow it all at once. It was the first proper meal he had tasted in many days, and it brought the strength back to his limbs like warm water poured into a cup. Then, with a little of his old courage restored, he began to think seriously about where he should go.

All around the pit, a strange red plant was growing, with thick stems and coarse leaves, in a tangle so dense that he had to force a path through it. It had already smothered the broken ground, and it was climbing over the walls of the ruined houses as if it meant to claim the whole district for itself. He had never seen anything like it, and he knew without being told that it had come from Mars.

The red weed followed the river for as far as he could see, and in places it grew right out across the water, so that the stream ran as thick and dark as wine. The whole valley had taken on a strange new colour, and the narrator felt like a traveller who has wandered by accident into another world. Only the hills in the distance remained green, and they seemed to him like islands in a sea that was slowly rising.

He turned toward London and walked for many hours along the empty road, past houses with their windows shut and their gardens run wild. There were no birds singing in the trees and no dogs barking in the yards, and the silence was almost harder to bear than the thunder of the Martian machines. Once he stopped and shouted aloud, simply to hear a human voice, but the sound died quickly and nothing answered him.

On Putney Hill, he saw a man sitting in the shade of a tree, and he stopped short, his heart beating hard with the old fear. The stranger was thin, dirty and wild-eyed, but as the narrator came closer, he recognised him with sudden astonishment and a rush of relief. It was the artilleryman, whom he had last seen on the night when the world was burning.

The artilleryman greeted him with a bitter laugh and said that humankind was beaten, and that the Martians would soon hunt down every man who was left. In his opinion, the survivors would be herded into cages and fed like cattle, kept alive only to serve the new masters of the Earth. He spoke calmly, like a man who had thought the matter through a hundred times and no longer felt any surprise.

Those who had lived soft lives in offices and suburbs, he declared, would not last a month, for only the strong and the wild had any chance now. The only safe refuge, he believed, lay beneath the ground, in the great drains and tunnels that ran under London like a second city. There a few hardy people could live out of sight, and wait, and grow in knowledge and in numbers.

The artilleryman's dream grew larger as he spoke, until it filled the whole of the hot morning with its lamps, its libraries, its machines and its chosen men and women. One day, he said, they would capture a Martian engine, and learn its secrets, and turn it against its makers. His eyes shone, and for a while the narrator was carried along by the sheer confidence of his voice.

But when he looked at what the artilleryman had actually done, he found only a shallow hole in the ground, scarcely deeper than a ditch, and a pack of cards lying on the grass. It dawned upon him that this was a man who loved to plan far more than he loved to work, and who would be no safer in his dream than in the open. So he said goodbye, with some sadness and some relief, and went on his way toward the silent city, where he hoped to find at least an answer.

The narrator walked into the great city of London, and he found it as empty and silent as a painted city on a stage. The shops were shut, the windows were dark, and his footsteps rang along the road with an echo that seemed to mock him. For the first time he understood what it would mean to be the last man alive in a world that had once been so crowded.

A thin film of black dust lay over the pavements and the roofs, the dried remains of the poison smoke that had rolled through the streets in the days of the terror. Nothing moved in all that quiet, not even a stray cat, and somewhere a door was swinging slowly on its hinges in the wind. The narrator walked in the middle of the road, because he feared the shadowed doorways more than he feared the open sky.

Then, from far ahead, there came a long, sad cry that rose and fell like the wail of a lost animal, and the words it seemed to say were ulla, ulla, ulla. He knew that sound, for he had heard it once before, far away across the dark fields, and a cold hand closed upon his heart. Yet there was something different in it now, something weaker and more broken than the cry that he remembered with dread.

The cry went on and on, rising and falling, and it seemed to come from no one place but from the whole dead city at once. Again and again the narrator stopped to listen, and each time he found that it told him nothing, except that something was still alive in those silent streets. The mystery tormented him, and yet it was better than the emptiness, for a sound, even a terrible sound, is a kind of company.

At last he sat down on a doorstep and thought of his wife, and of the quiet evenings that they had spent together in the lamplight, which he had been too busy to value. The loneliness was worse than any fear, and he knew that he could not endure it for long. Something in him, long numbed by horror, began slowly to wake and to ask what was the use of surviving if there was nobody to survive for.

He decided that he would rather meet the Martians face to face than live on alone and afraid in a dead city, and the decision lifted a weight from his spirit. If they killed him, he reasoned, at least the waiting would be over, and if they did not, he might learn something worth knowing. He rose to his feet, brushed the dust from his clothes, and walked on with a steadier step.

He walked with his hands held open and empty, so that anyone watching might see that he came as a man without weapons and without hope of resistance. The cry grew louder as he went on, and now it sounded broken and weak, like the voice of a singer who has sung all night and has nothing left. It echoed between the empty houses with a hollow, lonely beauty that moved him in spite of himself.

At the edge of Regent's Park, he saw a giant Martian machine towering above the treetops, black and still against the pale sky. His heart beat so hard that he could hear it, and he stopped behind a wall, waiting for the great engine to turn and see him. But the machine did not move, and, as he stood there, the long cry that had led him on across the city broke off and was heard no more.

For a long time he watched from his hiding place, hardly daring to breathe, but nothing stirred in the park except the leaves in the wind. Then a flock of dark birds wheeled out of the sky, circled the silent machine, and settled one by one upon its hood. Their boldness told him more than any sound could have done, for birds do not perch upon a living enemy.

At last he crept forward, inch by inch, until he could see inside the hood of the great machine, and there he found the Martian slumped and lifeless, its huge head hanging down. No gun and no army had struck it down, and no wound could be seen on its body, which was all the more astonishing. The narrator stood in the open with the sunlight on his face and laughed and wept at once, like a man who has been let out of prison.

He climbed to the top of Primrose Hill and found there a huge pit, and in it lay more of the Martians, still and silent, their great bodies curled in the shadows. No sound came from that place except the sigh of the wind in the long grass and the thin cry of a bird that circled overhead. It seemed to him that he was standing at the open grave of a nightmare.

From the crest of the hill, he looked out over London, and everywhere he saw the great machines standing motionless, their hoods open to the sky and their long arms hanging limp. Wherever his eyes rested, the invaders lay dead, and not one of them had been touched by any weapon that men had made. The whole vast army that had threatened the Earth had gone out like a flame in a few short days.

Dogs and birds had already come to feed upon the dead, and the narrator turned his eyes away from the sight with a shudder. It was a grim thing to see, yet he felt very little pity, for the memory of the last weeks was too fresh and too terrible. He remembered the burned towns and the fleeing crowds, and he found that he could not weep for the destroyers.

He remembered the soldiers and their guns, which had fought so bravely at Weybridge and had achieved so little against the machines. Nothing that mankind possessed had been able to stop the invaders for even a day, and yet here they lay, slain without a single wound that anyone could see. The narrator stood in bewilderment, asking himself what unseen hand had saved the world.

In the clear morning light, the great dome of St Paul's rose dark above a city that was free of smoke for the first time in days, and the sky behind it was full of pale gold. The narrator stood for a long while on the hill, looking at it, and the fear that had lived in him through so many nights began slowly to fade. It was the first beautiful thing that he had seen since the beginning of the nightmare.

Only later did the scientists explain what had almost certainly happened, and their answer was stranger than any legend: the Martians had been struck down by the smallest living things on Earth. These microbes, which are invisible to the eye and which cause sickness in human beings, were a deadly danger to creatures that had never met them before. The invaders, with all their wonderful machines, had no more defence against them than a child has against a flood.

Over thousands of years, mankind had learned to live among such germs, and many millions had died in the learning, until our bodies had grown able to resist them. The Martians, who had never met these enemies, had no defence at all, and within a few days of landing they began to sicken and weaken. It was a victory that no army could have won, and it had been won by the humblest of allies.

The red weed that the invaders had brought with them was also dying, and it faded from the hills of England in grey and brown patches, as if the same sickness had touched it. Within a few weeks, the strange plant had almost disappeared from the fields and the river banks. Where it had been, the old green of the English countryside crept back, slowly and without any fuss, as though nothing had ever happened.

The narrator sat down upon the grass and wept with relief, like a child, and for a long time he could not stop. As the morning went on, the city slowly began to wake, and he heard windows opening and voices calling and the first steps of a few frightened people in the streets. It was the sound of a great and wounded creature drawing breath after a long and terrible sleep.

Late in the day, a kind family found him wandering, ragged and filthy and half out of his wits, and they took him into their home without asking a single question. They gave him hot food, clean clothes and a soft bed, and he slept for many hours, deeply and without a single dream. When he woke, a woman was sitting beside him with a cup of tea, and she smiled as if she had known him all his life.

At the family's table, the narrator heard the news that had been slowly spreading across the world while he lay in the ruins and on the hill. The Martians, it seemed, had died in every place where they had landed, and the other cylinders had been found silent, their machines standing motionless and their occupants dead. He listened in a daze, as a man listens to a story about someone else's life, and he found that he could not yet believe it.

Within a few days, the trains began to run again, and the telegraph carried the good news to every corner of the earth. In the streets, strangers shook hands and laughed, and the bells of many churches rang out over towns that had been silent for weeks. It seemed that the whole world, which had been holding its breath, was at last allowed to breathe.

As soon as he was strong enough to travel, the narrator took a train toward Woking, with his heart full of a fear that he could not name. From the carriage window, he saw the countryside lying quiet in the sun, with the red weed withering on the banks and the green of the grass returning. He told himself that, whatever he found at the end of the journey, he would bear it, because he had borne worse.

He walked up the familiar road to his house and found the front door standing open, as if the place had been waiting for him all these weeks. The rooms were silent and dusty, and in his study everything was exactly as he had left it, even to the unfinished page that lay on the desk beside his pen. He stood there a long time, and the ordinary objects seemed to him more precious and more strange than anything he had seen in the whole nightmare.

He sat down at the desk, feeling that everything which had happened belonged to another man, and then he heard a step in the hall behind him. A voice spoke his name, softly and uncertainly, as one speaks to a ghost, and he turned around very slowly, afraid to hope. For a moment he could neither move nor speak, for the sight in the doorway was the one that he had hardly dared to dream of.

His wife was standing there, pale and thinner than he remembered but alive, and with a cry she ran across the room and into his arms. They held each other without a word, and the tears ran down both their faces, for there was nothing in the language that could say what they felt. In that moment he knew that he had been given back everything that really mattered, and his heart overflowed with a deep and quiet thankfulness.

In the weeks that followed, the machines of the Martians were put on show, and scientists from many countries studied them with intense and humble curiosity. Crowds queued for hours to look at the strange pale metal and the silent engines that had so nearly destroyed the world. Much was learned from them, but much remained a mystery, for the minds that had made them were gone.

People began to see that the Earth was small, and that life, with all its dangers, could come to it from far across the dark. The narrator wondered whether men would meet the Martians again, or whether, one day, human beings would travel to Mars and look back at the blue Earth in the sky. He did not know the answer, but the question no longer seemed foolish to him, and he turned it over often in the evenings.

In the months that followed, people seemed more careful of one another and kinder, as if they had learned how quickly everything can change. The narrator went back to his writing and his quiet days, and he was almost happy, though a shadow remained at the back of his mind. Yet sometimes, in the night, he dreamed of the tall black machines marching under a red sky, and he woke with his heart pounding and his wife's hand upon his arm.

Now, on quiet evenings, the narrator sits in his garden with his wife and watches the sun go down behind the roofs of the little town. He looks at the sun, the sky and the ordinary world with new eyes, and he understands how much that is precious we pass by without a thought. And so, grateful for every peaceful hour, he ends his story where he began it, in the calm of an English evening that no one can ever again take for granted.
